name: Joanna Macy
known: Scholar of Buddhism and systems thinking who created the Work That Reconnects, a group practice for facing ecological crisis.

profile.known: Scholar of Buddhism and systems thinking who created the Work That Reconnects.
timeline: Born in Los Angeles
Completes her PhD at Syracuse University on Buddhism and general systems theory
Publishes Despair and Personal Power in the Nuclear Age
Publishes Mutual Causality in Buddhism and General Systems Theory
Publishes Active Hope with Chris Johnstone
Dies
ideas: The Great Turning
The shift from an industrial growth society to a life-sustaining one, seen as already under way.
Honouring our pain for the world
Grief for the world is a sign of connection to it, and facing it together frees energy to act.
Deep time
Imagining ourselves in relationship with ancestors and future generations.
sources: Mutual Causality in Buddhism and General Systems Theory (1991)
ask: What do you grieve about the world, and what does that grief tell you about what you love?
What would someone seven generations from now thank you for?

name: Gerard Endenburg
known: Dutch engineer and business owner who turned sociocracy into a working method for companies, with consent and linked circles.

name: Marshall Rosenberg
known: Psychologist who created Nonviolent Communication: observations, feelings, needs and requests.

name: William Bridges
known: Writer on transitions who separated change (the event) from transition (the inner passage through endings and a neutral zone).

name: Carl Folke
known: Environmental scientist and a leading voice on resilience: how social and ecological systems absorb shocks and reorganize.

name: David Cooperrider
known: Co-creator of Appreciative Inquiry, which starts change from what already works.

name: Dean Spade
known: Lawyer and organizer whose writing on mutual aid shaped how communities support each other in crises.

name: Ezio Manzini
known: Design researcher who studies how communities design their own solutions, and how designers can support them.

name: Geoff Mulgan
known: Former head of Nesta and policy adviser who writes on public innovation and collective intelligence.

name: Howard Zehr
known: Criminologist often called the grandfather of restorative justice: repairing harm instead of only punishing it.

name: Jennifer Pahlka
known: Founder of Code for America and author of Recoding America, on why policy fails in delivery.

name: John Gaventa
known: Scholar of power who developed the Powercube: the spaces, levels and forms through which power works.

name: Jonathan Rowson
known: Philosopher, chess grandmaster and co-founder of Perspectiva, who writes on the metacrisis.

name: Marshall Ganz
known: Organizer and teacher of public narrative: the story of self, us and now that moves people to act together.

name: Michael Tushman
known: Organizational theorist who, with Charles O'Reilly, described the ambidextrous organization.

name: Nigel Cross
known: Design researcher who showed how designers think, by framing and reframing problems as they work.

name: Rebecca Solnit
known: Writer whose A Paradise Built in Hell shows that people in disasters mostly help each other.

name: Richard Strozzi-Heckler
known: Teacher of somatic leadership, bringing the body and martial arts practice into how leaders act.

profile.known: Baltic German biologist who gave us the Umwelt: each creature lives in its own world, made of the signs it can sense and act on.
timeline: Born in Keblaste, in what is now Estonia
Publishes Umwelt und Innenwelt der Tiere (The Environment and Inner World of Animals)
Founds the Institute for Umwelt Research at the University of Hamburg
Publishes A Foray into the Worlds of Animals and Humans, with its famous tick
Dies on Capri
ideas: Umwelt
The world as one organism experiences it: only the things it can sense and act on. A tick lives in a world of three signs: butyric acid, warmth and hair.
Functional circle
Perceiving and acting form a loop between an organism and the things around it, close to what cybernetics later called feedback.

questions.claim: Animals are subjects with their own worlds, not machines reacting to stimuli.
questions.who: Behaviourists and mechanistic physiologists of his time
questions.other: Talk of an animal's inner world cannot be tested; science should describe only behaviour.
questions.what: The view, going back to Descartes and strong in early twentieth-century physiology and behaviourism, that animals are complex mechanisms: a stimulus goes in, a response comes out, and there is no need to talk about what the animal experiences or what anything means to it.
more: The concept and the tick example
The stimulus-and-response view he argued against

questions.claim: Historians note that his holism was tied to anti-democratic views and, briefly, to sympathy with the early Nazi state, which he later distanced himself from.
questions.who: His defenders, citing his own letters
questions.other: Admirers argue the biology stands apart from the politics and has been taken up by people of every persuasion.
questions.what: This is a critique of Uexküll himself rather than of an idea. His holistic biology pictured the state as an organism whose parts should each keep to their function, a picture he used to argue against parliamentary democracy. In the early 1930s he briefly expressed sympathy for the new Nazi state.
osrc: Uexküll, letter of May 1933 on the persecution of Jews (as quoted on Wikipedia)
more: Anne Harrington, Reenchanted Science (Princeton University Press)
Holistic biology in Germany and its politics, including Uexküll
His Staatsbiologie and how his views shifted in 1933

sources: A Foray into the Worlds of Animals and Humans (1934; English 2010)
ask: What does your workplace look like in the Umwelt of someone who uses it?
Which signs do you not notice that others depend on?

name: Thomas Sebeok
known: Linguist and semiotician who founded zoosemiotics, the study of signs among animals, and helped launch biosemiotics.

profile.known: Danish biochemist at the University of Copenhagen and a founder of biosemiotics. Argued that life is built on sign relations, and that the capacity to interpret signs grows through evolution.
timeline: Born in Denmark
With Claus Emmeche, proposes code duality: life passes on both a digital code (DNA) and an analog one (the living organism)
Publishes En snegl på vejen in Danish
Its English edition, Signs of Meaning in the Universe, becomes a turning point for the field
Becomes the first President of the International Society for Biosemiotic Studies, serving until 2015
Publishes Biosemiotics: An Examination into the Signs of Life and the Life of Signs
Dies on 25 September, aged 77
ideas: Semiotic freedom
How many ways a living thing can respond to the same sign. It tends to grow through evolution, from bacteria following a chemical trail to animals reading each other.
Code duality
Life runs on two codes at once: the digital code of DNA, and the analog code of the living body that reads it and is shaped by its world.
Semiosphere
He stretched Yuri Lotman's word for a culture's world of signs to cover all life: every organism lives inside a web of signs made by others.

questions.claim: Even the simplest living things interpret signs. Meaning is part of biology from the start, not something added later by minds.
questions.other: The genetic code and other organic codes are fixed rules of correspondence. They need no interpreter, and interpretation appears only in more complex animals.
more: Barbieri's alternative, which split from Peircean biosemiotics
Overview of the field and its schools
questions.what: Code biology, developed by Marcello Barbieri, holds that life is built on organic codes such as the genetic code: fixed rules that match one set of molecules to another, like a dictionary. In his view these codes work without anyone interpreting them, and meaning in the full sense only arrives later, with animals that have minds.

questions.claim: Biology already speaks of genes as information, messages and codes. Taking that language seriously means admitting that something reads them.
questions.other: Information is a useful shorthand. The chemistry explains what happens, and calling it meaning adds nothing testable.
questions.what: Since the 1950s molecular biologists have described DNA as carrying information, genes as instructions, and cells as reading, copying and translating messages. Most biologists treat this language as a convenient metaphor for chemical processes rather than a claim that cells understand anything.
more: Whether talk of genetic information is literal or a metaphor

sources: Signs of Meaning in the Universe (1996)
His best-known book, Indiana University Press
Biosemiotics: An Examination into the Signs of Life and the Life of Signs (2008)
Emmeche, Favareau and Kull: Jesper Hoffmeyer 1942–2019
ask: Does a bacterium following sugar "interpret" anything, or is that just a figure of speech?
If meaning goes all the way down, what changes about how you treat other living things?
Where would you draw the line between a signal and a sign?

name: Kalevi Kull
known: Biologist and semiotician at the University of Tartu, a central figure in biosemiotics and ecosemiotics.

name: Terrence Deacon
known: Biological anthropologist who asks how meaning and purpose arise from physical processes (Incomplete Nature).

profile.known: American philosopher and scientist. Founded pragmatism and the modern theory of signs.
timeline: Born in Cambridge, Massachusetts
Begins three decades of work for the US Coast Survey
Publishes On a New List of Categories, the root of his sign theory
Publishes How to Make Our Ideas Clear, a founding text of pragmatism
Dies in Milford, Pennsylvania, poor and largely unpublished
ideas: Icon, index, symbol
Signs work by resemblance (a map), by real connection (smoke means fire) or by convention (a word).
Semiosis
Meaning is a three-way process between a sign, what it stands for and the interpretation it produces, which is itself a new sign.
Abduction
Reasoning to the best guess: forming a hypothesis that would explain a surprise.
Fallibilism
Any belief might be wrong, so inquiry never closes.

questions.claim: A sign is not just a word and a meaning: interpretation is a third part, and it keeps going.
questions.who: Followers of Saussure's signifier and signified
questions.other: A two-part model is simpler and was more useful for studying language as a system.
questions.what: Ferdinand de Saussure's model of the sign has two sides: the signifier (a sound or written form) and the signified (the concept it calls up), joined by convention within a language. It became the basis of structuralism in linguistics, anthropology and cultural studies.
more: Peirce's theory of signs (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
The three-part sign: sign, object, interpretant

sources: Peirce's theory of signs (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
How to Make Our Ideas Clear (1878)
ask: Which signs in your work are icons, which indexes, which symbols?
Where are you using abduction without calling it that?

name: Ferdinand de Saussure
known: Linguist whose model of the sign (signifier and signified) founded structuralism.

name: Yuri Lotman
known: Semiotician who founded the Tartu-Moscow school and coined the semiosphere, the space of signs a culture lives in.

name: Umberto Eco
known: Semiotician and novelist whose A Theory of Semiotics set out how codes and signs work.

name: Roland Barthes
known: Writer and semiotician whose Mythologies shows how culture passes off the made as natural.

name: Norbert Wiener
known: Mathematician who named cybernetics: the study of control and communication through feedback.

name: W. Ross Ashby
known: Psychiatrist and cybernetician behind the law of requisite variety.

name: Heinz von Foerster
known: Cybernetician who founded second-order cybernetics: the observer is part of the system observed.

name: Gordon Pask
known: Cybernetician whose conversation theory treated learning as a conversation between people and systems.

name: Stafford Beer
known: Management cybernetician who created the Viable System Model and led Chile's Project Cybersyn.

profile.known: Founder of management cybernetics and the Viable System Model, who led Chile's Project Cybersyn.
timeline: Born in London
Publishes Cybernetics and Management
Begins Project Cybersyn for Salvador Allende's government in Chile
Publishes Brain of the Firm
Publishes The Heart of Enterprise
Publishes Beyond Dispute, on team syntegrity
Dies
ideas: Viable System Model
Five linked functions any organization needs to stay viable in a changing environment.
The purpose of a system is what it does
Judge a system by its results, not its stated intentions.
Variety engineering
Matching the variety of responses to the variety of situations, by amplifying and filtering.
ask: Judged by what it does, what is your organization's purpose?
Where is information arriving too slowly to steer by?

name: Ilya Prigogine
known: Chemist who won the Nobel Prize for work on systems far from equilibrium that organize themselves.

name: Santa Fe Institute
known: Research institute in New Mexico that made complexity science a field, from economics to biology.

name: NECSI
known: Research institute in Cambridge, Massachusetts, studying complex systems and applying them to policy.

profile.known: Anthropologist and cybernetician. Linked mind, communication and ecology.
timeline: Born in England
Publishes Naven, from fieldwork in New Guinea
Takes part in the Macy conferences on cybernetics
Co-authors the double bind theory of schizophrenia
Publishes Steps to an Ecology of Mind
Publishes Mind and Nature
Dies in San Francisco
ideas: Double bind
A message that contradicts itself at two levels, with no way to step outside it.
Ecology of mind
Mind is a pattern across organism and environment, not something inside a head.
The difference that makes a difference
His definition of information.

questions.claim: Acting on narrow goals cuts through the loops that keep a whole system healthy.
questions.other: Purposeful action is how societies have solved hard problems, from sanitation to vaccines.
questions.what: Bateson's name for goal-directed thinking: picking a narrow aim and acting straight toward it, as engineering and planning do. In a 1967 talk, published as "Conscious Purpose versus Nature" in Steps to an Ecology of Mind, he argued that this way of thinking, applied to ecosystems and societies, cuts through the loops that keep them in balance.
more: Steps to an Ecology of Mind, Wikipedia
The 1972 collection that includes "Conscious Purpose versus Nature"

sources: Steps to an Ecology of Mind (1972)
ask: Where has a clear goal made a situation worse?
Where would you be lost without one?

name: Margaret Mead
known: Anthropologist who took part in the Macy conferences that shaped cybernetics.

name: Stuart Kauffman
known: Theoretical biologist at the Santa Fe Institute who studies self-organization and the origins of order.

episodes.title: The Latest from the Cynefin Centre

profile.known: Management consultant and researcher. Created the Cynefin framework.
timeline: Born in Wales
Develops Cynefin while at IBM
Founds Cognitive Edge, later The Cynefin Company
Publishes A Leader's Framework for Decision Making in Harvard Business Review, with Mary Boone
ideas: Cynefin
Different kinds of situation (clear, complicated, complex, chaotic) need different ways of acting.
Safe-to-fail probes
In complex situations, run small experiments and amplify what works.

questions.claim: Copying what worked elsewhere fails when cause and effect only show up in hindsight.
questions.other: Standard methods spread proven gains and cut costly variation.
questions.what: Best practice means finding the method that worked best somewhere and copying it everywhere: standard procedures, benchmarking, frameworks rolled out across an organization. It comes from engineering and quality management, where cause and effect are stable and repeatable.
questions.quote: best practice is, by definition, past practice
qsrc: Snowden and Boone, A Leader's Framework for Decision Making, HBR, Nov 2007 (as quoted on Wikipedia)
questions.oquote: Checklists established a higher standard of baseline performance.
osrc: Atul Gawande, The Checklist, The New Yorker, December 2007

questions.claim: Developmental stage models are often sold as ladders without enough evidence.
questions.who: Bill Torbert (developmental action inquiry), among vertical development practitioners
questions.other: Stage-based coaching gives people a language for growth that many find useful.
questions.what: Leadership versions of adult development stage theories, such as the "action logics" of William Torbert and David Rooke or the colour-coded organizations in Frederic Laloux's Reinventing Organizations. They sort leaders or organizations into developmental levels, often using assessments sold for coaching, hiring and promotion.
more: Coaches Rising, episode 161: Bill Torbert, A Response to Dave Snowden's Critique of Developmental Theory
Torbert answers the charges of elitism, linearity and stereotyping
Alexei Kapterev, What's wrong with theories of vertical development
A critic's summary of the research behind stage models

sources: A Leader's Framework for Decision Making (2007)
Cynefin: Weaving Sense-Making into the Fabric of Our World (2020)
ask: Can you name one situation from your work in each Cynefin domain?
When is a best practice exactly the right call?

name: Karl Weick
known: Organizational theorist of sensemaking and, with Kathleen Sutcliffe, of high reliability organizing.

profile.known: Organizational theorist of sensemaking and, with Kathleen Sutcliffe, of high reliability organizing.
timeline: Born in Indiana
Publishes The Social Psychology of Organizing
Publishes Educational Organizations as Loosely Coupled Systems
Publishes his study of the Mann Gulch fire disaster, on the collapse of sensemaking
Publishes Sensemaking in Organizations
Publishes Managing the Unexpected with Kathleen Sutcliffe
Dies
ideas: Sensemaking
How people turn confusing situations into something they can act on, often looking back.
Enactment
People help create the environments they then respond to.
Loose coupling
Parts of an organization that are connected but keep their own identity, which makes them adaptable.
Mindful organizing
Staying alert to small failures, refusing to simplify, and deferring to expertise.
sources: The Collapse of Sensemaking in Organizations: The Mann Gulch Disaster (1993)
Managing the Unexpected (2001, with Kathleen Sutcliffe)
ask: When did your team last make sense of something only after acting?
Which small failure are you explaining away?

name: Kurt Lewin
known: Psychologist who began action research and the T-group, and studied groups as fields of forces.

profile.known: Social psychologist who founded action research and the study of group dynamics.
timeline: Born in Mogilno, then in Prussia
Leaves Germany for the United States
With Ronald Lippitt and Ralph White, studies democratic and autocratic leadership climates
Founds the Research Center for Group Dynamics at MIT
Publishes Action Research and Minority Problems; a workshop he leads gives rise to the T-group
Dies
ideas: Field theory
Behaviour is a function of the person and their environment, a field of forces acting at once.
Action research
Research done with people, in cycles of planning, acting and reflecting.
Nothing as practical as a good theory
His own phrase for joining theory and practice.

questions.what: A three-step model of change widely taught in management courses and attributed to Lewin: loosen the current state, change it, then stabilize the new one.
questions.claim: Groups hold steady because forces balance in a field; change means shifting that balance, studied with the people involved.
questions.who: Stephen Cummings, Todd Bridgman and Kenneth Brown (2016)
questions.other: The tidy three-step model was largely built by later writers; Lewin never presented it as a simple recipe, and teaching it that way flattens his field theory.
more: Lewin, groups, experiential learning and action research (infed)

ask: What forces are holding your situation steady?
Who would need to take part for research on it to change anything?

profile.known: Brazilian educator. Linked literacy to people naming and changing their own conditions.
timeline: Born in Recife, Brazil
Literacy campaign in Angicos
Jailed and exiled after the military coup
Writes Pedagogy of the Oppressed
Returns to Brazil
Dies in São Paulo
ideas: Banking model
Education that deposits facts into passive learners. He argued against it.
Conscientização
Learning to see the social causes of your situation, and acting on them.

questions.claim: Treating learners as empty containers keeps them from questioning their conditions.
questions.who: E. D. Hirsch Jr. and other advocates of knowledge-rich, direct teaching
questions.other: Clear teaching of basics gives poorer students the tools wealthier ones already have.
questions.what: Freire's name for the familiar classroom model in which the teacher holds the knowledge and deposits it into students, who store, memorize and repeat it, like money in a bank. Students are judged on how well they keep what they were given.
questions.quote: the teacher issues communiqués and makes deposits which the students patiently receive, memorize, and repeat
qsrc: Paulo Freire, Pedagogy of the Oppressed, ch. 2, p. 58 (as quoted on Wikipedia)
more: Cultural literacy and the case for teaching shared knowledge directly
Freire's argument and responses to it

sources: Builds on Freire and questions the sexist language in his early work
ask: When did you last learn something by naming your own situation?
What does direct teaching do well?

name: Myles Horton
known: Co-founder of the Highlander Folk School, which trained labour and civil rights organizers through popular education.

name: bell hooks
known: Writer and teacher whose Teaching to Transgress brought engaged, liberating pedagogy into classrooms.

name: John Dewey
known: Philosopher of education who argued that we learn from experience only when we reflect on it.

name: David Kolb
known: Educational theorist known for the experiential learning cycle.

name: Donald Schön
known: Thinker on reflective practice: how professionals think in action in messy situations.

profile.known: Philosopher of professional practice who showed how practitioners think in action.
timeline: Born in Boston
Gives the BBC Reith Lectures, published in 1971 as Beyond the Stable State
Publishes Theory in Practice with Chris Argyris
Publishes The Reflective Practitioner
Publishes Educating the Reflective Practitioner
Dies
ideas: Reflection-in-action
Thinking about what you are doing while you do it, and adjusting.
The reflective practitioner
Professionals in messy situations learn by framing problems and testing moves, not by applying theory.
Learning systems
Organizations and societies need to become systems that keep learning as things change.
ask: When did you last change course in the middle of doing something?
How do you reframe a problem that will not budge?

name: Chris Argyris
known: Organizational theorist of single- and double-loop learning, and of defensive routines that block it.

profile.known: Organizational theorist of how people and organizations learn, and why smart people often fail to.
timeline: Born in Newark, New Jersey
Publishes Theory in Practice with Donald Schön
Publishes Organizational Learning with Donald Schön
Publishes 'Teaching Smart People How to Learn' in Harvard Business Review
Dies
ideas: Espoused theory and theory-in-use
What people say guides them often differs from what actually drives their behaviour.
Single- and double-loop learning
Fixing errors within the rules versus questioning the rules themselves.
Defensive routines
Habits that protect people from embarrassment but block learning.
Ladder of inference
How we climb from what we observe to conclusions, often without noticing.
sources: Teaching Smart People How to Learn (HBR, 1991)
ask: Where does what you say guide you differ from what you do?
Which rule would double-loop learning ask you to question?

name: Jack Mezirow
known: Founder of transformative learning theory: adults change their frame after a disorienting dilemma.

name: Robert Kegan
known: Developmental psychologist of adult meaning-making and, with Lisa Lahey, immunity to change.

name: Jean Piaget
known: Psychologist who described how children's thinking develops through stages.

name: Jean Lave
known: Anthropologist who, with Etienne Wenger, described learning as taking part in communities of practice.

name: Etienne Wenger
known: Educational theorist who developed the idea of communities of practice and social learning.

name: Reg Revans
known: Founder of action learning: small groups working on real problems through questions rather than advice.

name: Wilfred Bion
known: Psychoanalyst whose studies of groups founded the Group Relations tradition.

name: David Bohm
known: Physicist who proposed dialogue as a way for groups to notice the assumptions in their shared thinking.

profile.known: Physicist who proposed dialogue as a way for groups to see the assumptions in their shared thinking.
timeline: Born in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania
Publishes Quantum Theory and, after refusing to testify against colleagues, leaves the United States for Brazil
Proposes a hidden-variables interpretation of quantum mechanics
Publishes Wholeness and the Implicate Order
Dies in London
On Dialogue, edited by Lee Nichol, is published
ideas: Dialogue
A group thinking together, suspending assumptions instead of defending them.
Thought as a system
Thinking is collective and produces many of the problems it then tries to solve.
Implicate order
A deeper, enfolded order of wholeness from which the visible world unfolds.
ask: Which assumption would your team rather defend than look at?
What happens if you meet with no decision to make?

name: Otto Scharmer
known: Co-founder of the Presencing Institute and author of Theory U.

name: Peter Senge
known: Author of The Fifth Discipline, which popularized systems thinking and learning organizations.

name: Horst Rittel
known: Design theorist who, with Melvin Webber, named wicked problems.

name: Herbert Simon
known: Nobel economist and pioneer of decision science, bounded rationality and the sciences of design.

profile.known: Polymath of decision-making, organizations, artificial intelligence and design, who showed that people satisfice rather than optimize.
timeline: Born in Milwaukee, Wisconsin
Publishes Administrative Behavior
With Allen Newell, builds the Logic Theorist, an early AI program
Publishes The Architecture of Complexity
Publishes The Sciences of the Artificial
Receives the Nobel Prize in economics
Dies
ideas: Bounded rationality
People decide with limited information, time and attention, so they look for good enough rather than best.
Satisficing
Choosing the first option that meets your standard instead of searching for the optimum.
Near-decomposability
Complex systems are built from parts that interact more inside than between, which makes them understandable and evolvable.

questions.what: Standard economic models assume people and firms maximize their gains with full information and unlimited calculating power.
questions.claim: Real people and organizations cannot do this; theories should describe how they actually decide under limits.
questions.other: Theories should be judged by how well they predict, not by whether their assumptions are realistic; people may act as if they maximize.

ask: Where are you searching for the best answer when good enough would do?
Which parts of your system could change without disturbing the rest?

name: W. Brian Arthur
known: Economist at the Santa Fe Institute who founded complexity economics and studied increasing returns.

profile.known: Political economist. Showed how communities govern shared resources without state or market control.
timeline: Born in Los Angeles
Co-founds the Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis, Indiana University
Publishes Governing the Commons
First woman awarded the Nobel Prize in economics
Dies
ideas: Design principles
Eight features shared by long-lasting commons, such as clear boundaries and local rule-making.
Polycentric governance
Many overlapping centres of decision, rather than one.

questions.claim: Users of a shared resource don't inevitably ruin it; many communities have governed commons for centuries.
questions.who: Garrett Hardin, "The Tragedy of the Commons", Science, 1968
questions.other: Without a state or private owner, large open-access resources do get overused.
questions.what: An argument made by the ecologist Garrett Hardin in a 1968 essay in Science. He imagined a pasture open to all herders: each herder gains by adding one more animal, while the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone, so rational individuals end up ruining the pasture. He concluded that shared resources must be privatized or controlled by government.
questions.quote: the earlier theories of rational, but helpless, individuals who are trapped in social dilemmas are not supported by a large number of studies
qsrc: Elinor Ostrom, Nobel Prize lecture, 8 December 2009 (PDF)
questions.oquote: Freedom in a commons brings ruin to all.
osrc: Garrett Hardin, The Tragedy of the Commons (1968)
more: Background, and how Ostrom and others answered Hardin

sources: Garrett Hardin, The Tragedy of the Commons (1968)
ask: Do her principles hold at the scale of the climate?
Which commons do you share, and who makes its rules?

profile.known: Environmental scientist and systems thinker. Lead author of The Limits to Growth.
timeline: Born in Illinois
Lead author of The Limits to Growth
Publishes Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System
Dies
Thinking in Systems published after her death
ideas: Leverage points
Places in a system where a small shift produces big change. Goals and paradigms rank highest.
Stocks and flows
Most behaviour comes from what accumulates and how fast it fills and drains.

questions.claim: Growth in material use can't continue forever on a finite planet.
questions.other: Human ingenuity and prices find substitutes; the 1972 scenarios underrated innovation.
questions.what: The assumption that economies can and should keep increasing their output year after year. Most governments judge success by growth in GDP. The Limits to Growth (1972) used a computer model, World3, to explore what happens if population and industrial output keep growing exponentially on a finite planet.
questions.quote: Growth has costs as well as benefits, and we typically don't count the costs
qsrc: Donella Meadows, Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System (1999)
osrc: Julian Simon, The State of Humanity (1995), quoted in Reason, May 1998
more: The 1972 study, its critics, and later comparisons with real data

ask: Which of her leverage points have you seen used?
How would you test the growth argument yourself?

name: Fritjof Capra
known: Physicist and writer on living systems and ecological literacy (The Web of Life).

name: Grace Lee Boggs
known: Detroit activist and philosopher whose ideas on change shaped emergent strategy.

name: Octavia Butler
known: Science fiction writer whose Parable novels inspired emergent strategy and movement work.

name: Arnold van Gennep
known: Ethnographer who described rites of passage: separation, a threshold, and return.

name: Victor Turner
known: Anthropologist of liminality and communitas, the bond of people crossing a threshold together.

name: Enrico Quarantelli
known: Founder of disaster sociology, whose research showed people rarely panic in disasters.

name: W. Edwards Deming
known: Statistician and teacher of quality improvement: most problems come from the system, not the worker.

profile.known: Statistician and teacher of quality who argued that most problems come from the system, not the people working in it.
timeline: Born in Sioux City, Iowa
Lectures to Japanese engineers and managers on statistical quality control
The Deming Prize for quality is established in Japan
Featured in the NBC documentary 'If Japan Can... Why Can't We?'
Publishes Out of the Crisis, with his 14 points for management
Publishes The New Economics and dies the same year
ideas: System of profound knowledge
Four lenses for managing: appreciation of a system, knowledge of variation, theory of knowledge, and psychology.
Common and special causes
Most variation comes from the system itself; blaming individuals for it makes things worse.
Plan, do, study, act
Improve in small cycles of testing and learning.

questions.target: Merit rating and annual performance reviews
questions.what: Rating and ranking individual employees each year, often linked to pay, promotion or dismissal. It remains standard practice in many organizations.
questions.claim: Ranking individuals for results that mostly come from the system destroys teamwork and pride in work; he called it one of the deadly diseases of management.
questions.other: Clear individual goals and feedback motivate people, reward good work and make accountability possible.
more: His life and the seven deadly diseases

ask: Which problem are you blaming on people that the system is producing?
What would you stop measuring if you trusted the system view?

name: Michael Quinn Patton
known: Evaluator who created developmental evaluation for complex, changing programmes.

name: Orlando Fals-Borda
known: Colombian sociologist who founded participatory action research.

name: Vine Deloria Jr.
known: Standing Rock Sioux writer and scholar whose work defended Indigenous knowledge and sovereignty.

name: Robin Wall Kimmerer
known: Potawatomi botanist and author of Braiding Sweetgrass, joining Indigenous and scientific knowledge.

ideas: Three dimensions of power
Power shows in who wins decisions, in which issues never reach the table, and in shaping what people want in the first place.
Real interests
People can be led to accept arrangements that work against interests they would recognize with more knowledge or freedom.

questions.what: Robert Dahl's study of New Haven, Who Governs? (1961), measured power by who prevails when groups openly disagree over decisions. This pluralist view became the standard way to study power in political science.
questions.claim: Watching only open decisions misses most power: what is kept off the agenda, and how people come to want what keeps them quiet.
questions.who: Robert Dahl and pluralist political scientists
questions.other: Power has to be studied in observable conflict. Claims about people's 'real interests' that they do not themselves hold are hard to test and risk telling people what they should want.

ideas: Symmathesy
Living things learn and change together, in context. No part learns alone.
Warm Data
Information about how parts of a system relate, gathered across many contexts at once.
Transcontextual
A problem lives in many contexts at once: family, economy, health, culture.

questions.claim: Ranking people into higher and lower stages ignores context, and setting developmental goals for others is dangerous.
questions.quote: Stage theory... Is BS. Always was. And it is colonial as hell.
questions.quote2: dictating developmental goals for other people's lives, thoughts, and feelings is dangerous.
q2src: Nora Bateson, "Just for the record", Medium
questions.who: Emil Ejner Friis (co-author as Hanzi Freinacht)
questions.other: Stages are backed by research, and they help people judge less: a crude view comes from lacking support to grow, not from a flaw in the person.
questions.oquote: due to a lack of the privilege that supports growth, not to an inherent flaw of the person.
more: Jeff Salzman, The Daily Evolver: "The Great Stage-Theory Debate" (28 Oct 2021)
An integral-side podcast walking through both positions
A middle path: keep Graves' insights, drop the ranked stages
Benjamin P. Taylor, "There's been a kerfuffle about 'stage theory'"
Lays out the questions on both sides, with links
Background on Piaget, Kegan and others
questions.what: Stage theories say that the way people make sense of the world grows through a fixed sequence of stages, each able to hold more complexity than the one before. Jean Piaget described stages for children; Robert Kegan, Clare Graves (whose work became Spiral Dynamics) and Ken Wilber described them for adults. In leadership and "vertical development" programmes, people are sometimes assessed, placed at a stage, and coached to move "up".

questions.claim: Treating complex problems as things to fix with one intervention ignores how everything around them shifts in response.
questions.other: Without clear goals and measures, public money can't be accounted for and nothing gets tested.
questions.what: The habit of treating a complex problem like a fault in a machine: find the cause, design one intervention, roll it out, and check whether a target number moved. It sits behind most programme funding, logframes and results-based management.
questions.quote: the resulting solutions that do not address the complexity seem only to generate more consequences
more: What she proposes instead of predetermined solutions
The goals-and-measures approach the other side defends

sources: Her essays, in her own words
Robert Kegan, In Over Our Heads (1994)
The main stage view she pushes against
ask: Have you seen a stage model help someone? Have you seen one used to rank people?

ideas: Autopoiesis
A living system is a network that continually produces itself.
Structural coupling
Organisms and environments change together through repeated interaction.
Love as acceptance
Love as accepting the other as a legitimate other in living together, the basis of social life.

questions.what: The sociologist Niklas Luhmann built a theory of society in which social systems are autopoietic: they reproduce themselves through communication, not through people.
questions.claim: Autopoiesis describes living cells; societies are networks of living beings in language, not autopoietic systems themselves.
questions.other: Social systems reproduce their own communications in a closed network, so autopoiesis is exactly the right concept for them.
more: The concept and its uses beyond biology

sources: With Francisco Varela, the most readable introduction
